```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cleanTMLE)
```

This vignette is for two readers: the analyst who writes the plan, and the
review team who reads the dossier and decides whether to admit the outcome.
It assumes you have run "Get started with cleanTMLE".

Everything in the plan is fixed when the lock is created. Choose each part
with the study question in front of you, not the data, and write down why;
the plan is part of the record the review team reads.

## Writing the plan

### The estimand ladder

`estimands` lists the estimands you would accept, in order of preference.
The first one the design can support becomes the primary estimand, and the
others are reported as secondary. Put first the estimand that answers the
study question. If the question is about the whole population, that is the
average treatment effect (ATE). Then list the estimands you would accept
instead, knowing that each describes a different population: the trimmed
ATE [@crump2009trimming], the average treatment effect among the treated
(ATT), and the overlap-weighted effect (ATO) [@li2018overlap], as defined
in "Get started with cleanTMLE".

If one of these would not answer a question anyone cares about, leave it
off the ladder. A ladder that ends in an estimand nobody will use only
postpones the decision. `trim_band` is required when the trimmed ATE is on
the ladder; 0.05 to 0.95 and 0.1 to 0.9 are common choices.

### Tolerances

An estimand is feasible when an estimator meets the tolerances on every
simulated outcome surface. `tolerance$bias` is the largest absolute bias you
would accept, on the risk difference scale; set it well below the smallest
effect that would matter clinically. `tolerance$coverage` is the lowest
coverage of the 95% confidence interval you would accept.

`tolerance$ci_halfwidth` is optional. With it, an estimand is feasible only
if its expected interval is narrow enough to be informative. Use it when a
precise but uninformative answer would not be worth reporting.

### The outcome surfaces

The design stage cannot use the real outcome, so it runs a plasmode
simulation: it tests each estimator against simulated outcomes drawn from a
family of outcome models fixed in the plan, the outcome surfaces.
The family varies the baseline risk (`baseline_risk`), the treatment effect
on the log-odds scale (`log_or`), how much that effect changes with the
propensity score (`heterogeneity`), how strongly the covariates predict the
outcome (`prognostic`), and whether that relationship is linear or not
(`forms`). The vectors you give are crossed into a grid, and an effect that
does not change with the propensity score (heterogeneity 0) is always
included. With the default two forms, the plan below has 2 x 2 x 3 x 2
surfaces, and `analysis_plan()` says so:

```{r grid}
p <- analysis_plan("y", "ATE", time_zero = "treatment assignment",
                    surfaces = list(log_or = c(0, 0.5), heterogeneity = c(0.5, 1),
                                    prognostic = c(0.5, 1)))
p$surfaces[c("log_or", "heterogeneity", "prognostic", "forms")]
```

Heterogeneity that tracks the propensity score is what separates the ATE,
ATT and ATO, and what punishes an estimator that extrapolates; keep at least
one non-zero value. A larger grid makes the check stricter, because an
estimand must pass on every surface, and slower, because every candidate is
fit on each.

Feasibility is supported only over this family. A design can fail on an
outcome model outside it, and the dossier says so. If a data steward who is
not on the analysis team can fit a risk model on the covariates alone, its
predictions can be passed as `surfaces$q0` to make the family closer to the
real outcome without anyone on the team seeing it.

### Candidates and learners

`ps_library` fits the propensity score, and `candidates` lists the outcome
models and the truncation levels for the propensity score that the design
stage compares. The default library uses one learner of each kind: an
elastic net, multivariate adaptive regression splines, gradient-boosted
trees, and a small neural network. The design stage picks, for each
feasible estimand, the candidate with the smallest worst-case error across
the surfaces, and `estimate_effect()` later uses exactly that candidate.

### Repetitions and Monte Carlo error

`reps` is the number of simulated datasets per surface. Each verdict is an
estimate with Monte Carlo error, so the dossier reports an interval for
every bias and coverage and marks a cell unresolved when its interval
contains a tolerance. With `max_reps` above `reps`, unresolved cells that
could change the decision get more repetitions. The Monte Carlo standard
error of a coverage near 0.95 shrinks with the square root of the number of
repetitions:

```{r mcse}
reps <- c(50, 200, 1000)
data.frame(reps = reps, mcse_coverage = round(sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / reps), 3))
```

### Negative controls

`negative_controls` names outcomes that treatment should not affect, each
with a domain describing the kind of confounding it can detect, such as
health care use. The control is estimated for every estimand on the ladder,
on the full cohort and on each of the `restrictions`, and graded against
`nc_criteria`. Each estimand's control is fitted with the candidate the
simulation selected for it, so the check tests the adjustment the analysis
will use; for an estimand the simulation found infeasible, it uses the
candidate with the smallest worst-case error and the table says so. With the default interval rule, the verdict for an
estimand is GO when every control's 95% interval lies inside the null band,
STOP when any lies entirely outside it, and FLAG otherwise, which includes
an interval too wide to tell and too few estimable controls. Only the
verdict for the primary estimand on the full cohort can block unblinding.
The rules `"point"` (the point estimate inside the band) and `"ci"` (the
interval inside the band, with anything else a failure) are stricter.

A control must not be one of the adjustment covariates, and
`create_analysis_lock()` stops if it is, because a control regressed on
itself has an estimate near zero by construction and would read GO. The same
holds for a control derived from a covariate under another name, such as
"cooking with wood or charcoal" derived from "cooking fuel". The lock
cannot see that link, so name the source in `nc_exclude`, a list from each
control to the covariates to leave out when that control is fitted:

```r
analysis_plan(
  outcome = "death_30d", estimands = "ATE", time_zero = "treatment assignment",
  negative_controls = c(wood_or_charcoal = "household environment"),
  nc_exclude = list(wood_or_charcoal = "cooking_fuel"))
```

The control is then adjusted for every other covariate. The dossier lists
the covariates left out of each control. The plan in this vignette has no
derived control, so it needs no exclusion.

Choose the null band as you would the bias tolerance: the largest residual
bias you would accept. A null band narrower than the precision your cohort
allows will give FLAG; that is information for the review team, not a
failure.

### Roles

`roles` records who is the analyst, the data steward and the reviewers.
They appear in the dossier and the design log, and the lock's hash covers
them.

### The variable dictionary

The lock also takes a variable dictionary, with one row for each column it
keeps. Each row says where the column was recorded, whether it was recorded
only for patients reached at follow-up, when it was recorded and when the
attribute it describes was fixed (both before, at or after time zero), and
how the analysis uses it. Age is recorded after injury but fixed before it;
a heart rate on arrival is fixed after treatment is assigned. The lock stops
on a covariate fixed after time zero, on a treatment not fixed at time zero,
and on a column from the follow-up source that is neither an
outcome-observation indicator nor a negative control. A stand-in covariate,
an outcome-observation indicator, a follow-up negative control and a
restriction variable fixed after time zero each need a written `reason` in
their row. The lock checks that the response is there, not that it is
adequate, and it cannot check that the declared timings are true. The
dictionary for the example cohort is:

```{r dictionary}
knitr::kable(cr_example$dictionary[, c("column", "source", "recorded", "fixed", "role")])
```

## Reading the dossier

The dossier is what the review team approves. Each of its sections answers
one question.

### Decision

Which estimand is primary, and is that decision settled? If
the decision rests on unresolved cells, the simulation could not tell
whether an estimator met a tolerance; ask for more repetitions before
approving.

### Prespecified plan

Was the plan sensible before anyone saw the data?
Check that the ladder starts with the estimand the question needs, that the
tolerances are tight enough to matter, and that the outcome surfaces
include effect heterogeneity.

### Design

How good is the overlap? A poor grade, a c-statistic near 1, or a largest
weight in the tens or hundreds says the ATE depends on a few patients.

### Who each estimand describes

If the ladder moved, is the population the
primary estimand describes one the study question cares about? A trimmed
population that leaves out the sickest patients answers a different
question from the one the protocol asked.

### Simulation

For the primary estimand, how large are the bias and the
interval half-width? A feasible estimand with a wide interval may not be
worth estimating. The expected events show how much information each arm
will carry.

### Negative controls

Is the verdict for the primary estimand GO or FLAG?
A FLAG with a wide interval means the check could not rule out residual
confounding; say so in the report.

### Notes

What the simulation supports, and any caveats.

When the review team approves, `unblind()` records who approved and when.
If it refuses, because no estimand is feasible or the negative control says
STOP, proceeding needs an `override` with a written reason, and the reason
goes into the record.

## The design log

`export_design_log()` returns the full record as a JSON file, or with
`format = "muntner"` as the decision log of @muntner2024staging, with one
row per decision: the lock, the design assessment, the simulation verdict
for each estimand, the negative control, the pre-outcome decision, the
approval and any override, and each estimate. Release it with the paper.
